items.title: Satyagraha and the art of dissent in Kerala: A veteran journo visits her old haunt in Tvm
items.summary: The old Secretariat Building in the heart of Thiruvananthapuram has an iconic entrance called the Satyagraha Gate. It is here that hundreds of protestors have gathered over the years. They came from different parts of the state, had different agendas, different political affiliations, and demands. On any given day, one can see protestors sitting under a makeshift canopy, holding up placards or raising slogans. During quiet breaks, they would be eating a simple meal or sleeping on a mat. If the protests are big, they can block the arterial MG (Mahatma Gandhi) Road, which stretches in front of the Secretariat. Sometimes, they can get violent too. During my years as a journalist in Thiruvananthapuram, I had interviewed a variety of satyagrahis sitting in protest at the gates. They ranged from fisherfolk and teachers, to headload workers and political dissidents. Sometimes, my car got stuck in the middle of a swelling ocean of sloganeering satyagrahis who would be amused to see the rare sight of a woman driver. They would knock on my window and ask me to get out of the car and join them. Kerala is unique in many ways. The world’s first democratically elected communist government was formed here in 1957 under EMS Namboodiripad. It came into power without revolution or violence, but through a free multi-party election. Even though it was dismissed by the Union government two years later and replaced with President’s rule, the democratically elected communist government in Kerala stands in the records as the first of its kind. It also brought in its wake revolutionary social reform, which brought about dramatic changes in what was once an oppressively feudal society. Over the next couple of decades, satyagraha had become a way of life. “Thozhilali (worker) Zindabad” and “Inquilab Zindbad” were cries often heard on the streets. The protesting groups could be any size. They could belong to any religion, community, or political party. We could even sometimes see a couple of flag waving protestors standing outside a small business like a cloth shop demanding their rights. Satyagraha was a part of daily life. And then, the Gulf and the tourism booms happened. Trade unions slowly began to fade away as privatisation took over and more jobs opened up. items.title: Three AISA HCU students on indefinite hunger strike for fellowship hike, menstrual leave
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Three students of the University of Hyderabad have launched an indefinite hunger strike over six key demands to the university administration, including menstrual leave, a fellowship hike, and gender-sensitisation workshops. The students – Srestha, Sidhant, and Riya – are all members of the Left student organisation, All India Students' Association (AISA). The students have been sitting at the North Shopcom on hunger strike, which entered its fourth day on August 23. They have made the following demands to the university administration: > Menstrual leave and bodily dignity > Rs 3,000 University of Hyderabad Student Assistance (UoHSA) fellowship for every eligible student, without the 1,200-recipient cap > An end to the backlog and 75% attendance barriers in UoHSA > Meaningful attendance relaxation for chronically ill and disabled students > Mandatory and meaningful gender-sensitisation workshops > Remedial classes and academic support for students facing structural inequalities The protesting students have also criticised the administration for not allowing them to bring in tents to set up shelter to continue their strike. An AISA member from UoH, Srijan, said that the students had to temporarily shift back to their hostels on the night of August 22 as their makeshift tarpaulin tents couldn’t withstand heavy rain. The students shifted back to the hunger strike site on August 23. AISA HCU said the administration has not responded clearly to any of their demands. On August 22, a Medical Officer was sent to check on the hunger strikers, who advised ORS due to declining sugar levels, a statement from AISA said, adding that the administration was “threatening police intervention and force-feeding in the name of ‘procedure’.” The University Registrar also sent security personnel to ask the hunger strikers to meet him in his cabin for a discussion, AISA said. Instead, they demanded that the Registrar must visit the site of the hunger strike and engage in a dialogue with the students. The hunger strike was launched soon after a visit to the campus on August 17 by AISA national president Neha Bora, who maintained a hunger strike for 23 days at Jantar Mantar against the NEET paper leak, along with two other AISA members, Manish Kumar, and Aameen Amitoj, along with climate and education activist Sonam Wangchuk. items.title: ISRO to privatise launch vehicle production, ex-chief Madhavan Nair questions viability
items.summary: Former ISRO chairman G Madhavan Nair has questioned the viability of the Union government’s move to have private companies and public sector undertakings (PSUs) take over the manufacture of launch vehicles, arguing that industry already handles much of the manufacturing for ISRO, while the space agency continues to carry out critical operations such as final assembly, integration, testing, and launching. Madhavan Nair’s comments come after Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) Chairman Pawan Goenka said ISRO would stop manufacturing launch vehicles, with their production to be taken up by the private sector or PSUs. “ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU,” Goenka said while speaking at Business Today’s India @ 100 Economy Summit. According to Madhavan Nair, industry has already been involved in the manufacture of launch vehicles for decades, and “around 90% of the work” on rockets such as the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is currently done by industry. “The final assembly, integration, testing, and launching is done by ISRO. So that's the critical operation, and we cannot leave it to an industry who is not experienced or who does not have the expertise in the field,” he said. Madhavan Nair questioned whether private companies would be willing to make the investment required to independently undertake such operations. “If you want to create an establishment similar to ISRO, today it will cost something like 50,000 crores. And the income from that will be hardly a few thousand crores,” he said. “So which industry will come forward in making such a large investment with a very miniscule return? So that's a big question mark,” he added. According to Madhavan Nair, the more lucrative opportunities in the space sector lie in applications based on space technology rather than the manufacture of launch vehicles and satellites. “The contribution of the global business in space is only 20% from the hardware industry, whereas 80% is coming from the application program,” he said, pointing to services based on communication satellites and earth observation as examples.
